claim: The Pro47Ser variant of p53 (S47) exists in African-descent populations.
source: The Pro47Ser variant of p53 (S47) exists in African-descent populations and is associated with increased cancer risk in humans and mice.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The S47 variant is associated with increased cancer risk in humans and mice.
source: The Pro47Ser variant of p53 (S47) exists in African-descent populations and is associated with increased cancer risk in humans and mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: S47 cells show increased glutathione (GSH) accumulation compared to cells with wild-type p53.
source: Due to impaired repression of the cystine importer Slc7a11, S47 cells show increased glutathione (GSH) accumulation compared to cells with wild -type p53.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mice containing the S47 variant display increased mTOR activity.
source: We show that mice containing the S47 variant display increased mTOR activity and oxidative metabolism, as well as larger size, improved metabolic efficiency, and signs of superior fitness.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by western blot and immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1.

claim: Mice containing the S47 variant display increased oxidative metabolism.
source: We show that mice containing the S47 variant display increased mTOR activity and oxidative metabolism, as well as larger size, improved metabolic efficiency, and signs of superior fitness.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Seahorse analysis data in Figure 2.

claim: Mice containing the S47 variant are larger in size.
source: We show that mice containing the S47 variant display increased mTOR activity and oxidative metabolism, as well as larger size, improved metabolic efficiency, and signs of superior fitness.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by body composition data in Figure 6A.

claim: Mice containing the S47 variant show improved metabolic efficiency.
source: We show that mice containing the S47 variant display increased mTOR activity and oxidative metabolism, as well as larger size, improved metabolic efficiency, and signs of superior fitness.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by CLAMS data in Figure 6B.

claim: Mice containing the S47 variant show signs of superior fitness.
source: We show that mice containing the S47 variant display increased mTOR activity and oxidative metabolism, as well as larger size, improved metabolic efficiency, and signs of superior fitness.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by treadmill exercise data in Figure 6C-G.

claim: mTOR and its positive regulator Rheb display increased association in S47 cells.
source: Mechanistically, we show that mTOR and its positive regulator Rheb display increased association in S47 cells; this is due to an altered redox state of GAPDH in S47 cells that inhibits its ability to bind and sequester Rheb.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by PLA and IP-western data in Figure 4.

claim: The increased mTOR-Rheb association in S47 cells is due to an altered redox state of GAPDH that inhibits its ability to bind and sequester Rheb.
source: Mechanistically, we show that mTOR and its positive regulator Rheb display increased association in S47 cells; this is due to an altered redox state of GAPDH in S47 cells that inhibits its ability to bind and sequester Rheb.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by BMH crosslinking and IP-western data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Compounds that decrease glutathione normalize GAPDH-Rheb complexes in S47 cells.
source: Compounds that decrease glutathione normalize GAPDH-Rheb complexes and mTOR activity in S47 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by PLA and IP-western data in Figure 5.

claim: Compounds that decrease glutathione normalize mTOR activity in S47 cells.
source: Compounds that decrease glutathione normalize GAPDH-Rheb complexes and mTOR activity in S47 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: Mutations in the TP53 gene occur in more than 50% of human cancers.
source: Mutations in the TP53 gene occur in more than 50% of human cancers, and this gene is well known as the most frequently mutated gene in cancer (Hollstein et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Hollstein et al., 1991.

claim: TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in cancer.
source: Mutations in the TP53 gene occur in more than 50% of human cancers, and this gene is well known as the most frequently mutated gene in cancer (Hollstein et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Hollstein et al., 1991.

claim: p53 suppresses uncontrolled cellular growth and proliferation through apoptosis, senescence, cell cycle arrest, and ferroptosis.
source: p53 works to suppress uncontrolled cellular growth and proliferation through various pathways including apoptosis, senescence, cell cycle arrest, and ferroptosis (Stockwell et al., 2017; Vousden and Prives, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Stockwell et al., 2017 and Vousden and Prives, 2009.

claim: p53 regulates mitochondrial function, autophagy, cellular redox state, and the control of lipid and carbohydrate metabolism.
source: The metabolic functions of p53 include the regulation of mitochondrial function, autophagy, cellular redox state, and the control of lipid and carbohydrate metabolism; for review see Berkers et al., 2013; Gnanapradeepan et al., 2018.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to review articles.

claim: p53 negatively regulates the activity of mTOR.
source: As an integral part of its control of metabolism, p53 negatively regulates the activity of mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin), which is a master regulator of metabolism in the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: mTOR is a master regulator of metabolism in the cell.
source: As an integral part of its control of metabolism, p53 negatively regulates the activity of mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin), which is a master regulator of metabolism in the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge.

claim: mTOR is a serine-threonine protein kinase that is stimulated by mitogenic signals.
source: mTOR is a serine-threonine protein kinase that is stimulated by mitogenic signals, and phosphorylates downstream targets that in turn regulate protein synthesis and cell growth (Ben-Sahra and Manning, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Ben-Sahra and Manning, 2017.

claim: mTOR phosphorylates downstream targets that regulate protein synthesis and cell growth.
source: mTOR is a serine-threonine protein kinase that is stimulated by mitogenic signals, and phosphorylates downstream targets that in turn regulate protein synthesis and cell growth (Ben-Sahra and Manning, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Ben-Sahra and Manning, 2017.

claim: mTORC1 is primarily responsible for cell growth and protein synthesis.
source: mTOR exists in two distinct signaling complexes: mTORC1 is primarily responsible for cell growth and protein synthesis, while mTORC2 plays roles in growth factor signaling, cytoskeletal control, and cell spreading (Liu and Sabatini, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Liu and Sabatini, 2020.

claim: mTORC2 plays roles in growth factor signaling, cytoskeletal control, and cell spreading.
source: mTOR exists in two distinct signaling complexes: mTORC1 is primarily responsible for cell growth and protein synthesis, while mTORC2 plays roles in growth factor signaling, cytoskeletal control, and cell spreading (Liu and Sabatini, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Liu and Sabatini, 2020.

claim: mTOR activity is frequently upregulated in a diverse range of cancers.
source: Not surprisingly, mTOR activity is frequently upregulated in a diverse range of cancers.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: p53 negatively regulates the mTOR pathway through transactivation of PTEN, TSC2, PRKAB1 and SESN1/SESN2.
source: p53 negatively regulates the mTOR pathway in part through transactivation of the target genes PTEN, TSC2, PRKAB1 and SESN1/SESN2 (Budanov and Karin, 2008; Feng et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Budanov and Karin, 2008 and Feng et al., 2005.

claim: The regulation of mTOR by p53 couples the control of genome integrity with the decision to proliferate.
source: The regulation of mTOR by p53 is believed to couple the control of genome integrity with the decision to proliferate (Hasty et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Hasty et al., 2013.

claim: The Pro47Ser SNP (rs1800371, G/A) exists predominantly in African-descent populations.
source: A naturally occurring SNP in TP53 exists at codon 47, encoding serine instead of a proline (Pro47Ser, rs1800371, G/A). This variant exists predominantly in African-descent populations, and occurs in roughly 1% of African Americans and 6% of Africans from sub-Saharan Africa (Murphy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Murphy et al., 2017.

claim: The Pro47Ser variant occurs in roughly 1% of African Americans.
source: This variant exists predominantly in African-descent populations, and occurs in roughly 1% of African Americans and 6% of Africans from sub-Saharan Africa (Murphy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Murphy et al., 2017.

claim: The Pro47Ser variant occurs in roughly 6% of Africans from sub-Saharan Africa.
source: This variant exists predominantly in African-descent populations, and occurs in roughly 1% of African Americans and 6% of Africans from sub-Saharan Africa (Murphy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Murphy et al., 2017.

claim: The S47 variant is associated with increased risk for pre-menopausal breast cancer in African American women.
source: The S47 variant is associated with increased risk for pre-menopausal breast cancer in African American women (Murphy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Murphy et al., 2017.

claim: The S47 mouse develops markedly increased incidence of spontaneous cancer, particularly hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: In a mouse model, the S47 mouse develops markedly increased incidence of spontaneous cancer, particularly hepatocellular carcinoma (Jennis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Jennis et al., 2016.

claim: The S47 variant is defective in the regulation of p53 target genes that play roles in ferroptosis sensitivity, including SLC7A11.
source: This variant is likewise defective in the regulation of the small subset of p53 target genes that play roles in ferroptosis sensitivity, including the cystine importer SLC7A11.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by prior published work.

claim: Increased levels of cysteine and glutathione (GSH) accumulate in cells from S47 humans and mice.
source: As a result, increased levels of cysteine and glutathione (GSH) accumulate in cells from S47 humans and mice (Jennis et al., 2016; Leu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Jennis et al., 2016 and Leu et al., 2019.

claim: The ferroptotic defect in S47 mice leads to iron accumulation in their livers, spleens, and macrophages.
source: More recently, we showed that the ferroptotic defect in S47 mice leads to iron accumulation in their livers, spleens, and macrophages.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and refers to recently published work.

claim: The S47 variant is positively associated with markers of iron overload in African Americans.
source: We also showed that the S47 variant is positively associated with markers of iron overload in African Americans (Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Singh et al., 2020.

claim: Women carrying tumor-predisposing mutations in the BRCA1 gene tend to be physically larger and show increased fertility.
source: As an example, women carrying tumor-predisposing mutations in the BRCA1 gene tend to be physically larger and show increased fertility (Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Smith et al., 2012.

claim: S47 LCLs show modestly decreased expression of SESN1 and PTEN relative to WT LCLs following cisplatin treatment.
source: We confirmed via qRT-PCR that S47 LCLs show modestly decreased expression of the p53 target genes SESN1 and PTEN, and decreased transactivation of PRKAB1, relative to WT LCLs following cisplatin treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: S47 LCLs show decreased transactivation of PRKAB1 relative to WT LCLs following cisplatin treatment.
source: We confirmed via qRT-PCR that S47 LCLs show modestly decreased expression of the p53 target genes SESN1 and PTEN, and decreased transactivation of PRKAB1, relative to WT LCLs following cisplatin treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: S47 LCLs and MEFs show increased p-S6K1 (Thr389) compared to WT cells.
source: Western blot analysis of WT and S47 LCLs, along with multiple clones of WT and S47 MEFs, revealed increased p-S6K1 (Thr389) in S47 cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1A.

claim: The increase in p-S6K1 in S47 cells ranges between two- and threefold when normalized to total S6K1.
source: Following normalization to total S6K1, this increase ranged between two- and threefold (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by densitometry data in Figure 1B.

claim: S47 lung and skeletal muscle show increased levels of p-S6K1 (T389) and p-mTOR (Ser2448) relative to WT tissues.
source: We found increased levels of p-S6K1 (T389) and p-mTOR (Ser2448) in S47 lung and skeletal muscle, relative to WT tissues (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Increased mTOR activity was not seen in all tissues of the S47 mouse.
source: Interestingly, increased mTOR activity was not seen in all tissues of the S47 mouse (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and lung and skeletal muscle were the most consistently different between WT and S47.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Lung and skeletal muscle were the most consistently different between WT and S47 mice in terms of mTOR activity.
source: Interestingly, increased mTOR activity was not seen in all tissues of the S47 mouse (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and lung and skeletal muscle were the most consistently different between WT and S47.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There are no significant differences in p-AKT (Ser473) in WT and S47 lung tissue.
source: We also did not detect significant differences in p-AKT (Ser473) in WT and S47 lung tissue, suggesting that mTORC1 and not mTORC2 is likely responsible for the observed differences in mTOR activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: mTORC1 and not mTORC2 is likely responsible for the observed differences in mTOR activity between WT and S47 tissues.
source: We also did not detect significant differences in p-AKT (Ser473) in WT and S47 lung tissue, suggesting that mTORC1 and not mTORC2 is likely responsible for the observed differences in mTOR activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is an inference based on the p-AKT data.

claim: S47 MEFs show increased induction of markers of mTOR activation after serum re-feed compared to WT cells.
source: S47 cells consistently showed increased induction of markers of mTOR activation after serum re-feed compared to WT cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1G.

claim: S47 LCLs show increased OCR under stressed conditions compared to WT.
source: Seahorse analyses revealed that S47 LCLs show increased OCR under stressed conditions compared to WT (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 2A.

claim: Human S47 LCLs and mouse S47 MEFs show increased basal and compensatory glycolysis compared to WT cells.
source: These analyses also revealed that human S47 LCLs and mouse S47 MEFs show increased basal and compensatory glycolysis, compared to WT cells (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 2B and C.

claim: S47 LCLs and MEFs show significantly increased consumption of glucose and glutamine compared to WT cells.
source: These analyses revealed that S47 LCLs and MEFs show significantly increased consumption of glucose and glutamine, along with increased production of lactate and glutamate, compared to WT cells (Figure 2D and E)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by YSI analyzer data in Figure 2D and E.

claim: S47 LCLs and MEFs show increased production of lactate and glutamate compared to WT cells.
source: These analyses revealed that S47 LCLs and MEFs show significantly increased consumption of glucose and glutamine, along with increased production of lactate and glutamate, compared to WT cells (Figure 2D and E)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by YSI analyzer data in Figure 2D and E.

claim: LCLs from individuals heterozygous for the S47 variant show metabolite values typically intermediate between homozygous WT and S47 cells.
source: Interestingly, LCLs from individuals heterozygous for the S47 variant (S47/WT), and MEFs from S47/WT mice, showed values typically intermediate between homozygous WT and S47 cells (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 2D and E.

claim: S47 MEFs show a higher contribution of glucose carbon into the TCA cycle compared to WT cells.
source: Analysis of 13C6-glucose tracing in WT and S47 MEFs provided evidence for a higher contribution of glucose carbon into the TCA cycle in S47 cells compared to WT cells, as evidenced by increased labeling of citrate, malate, aspartate, and glutamate in S47 MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: S47 MEFs show increased labeling of citrate, malate, aspartate, and glutamate from 13C-glucose.
source: Analysis of 13C6-glucose tracing in WT and S47 MEFs provided evidence for a higher contribution of glucose carbon into the TCA cycle in S47 cells compared to WT cells, as evidenced by increased labeling of citrate, malate, aspartate, and glutamate in S47 MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: There is no obvious increase in mitochondrial content in S47 cells.
source: However, MitoTracker analyses and western blotting for mitochondrial proteins revealed no obvious increase in mitochondrial content in S47 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MitoTracker and western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: S47 LCLs and MEFs do not proliferate more quickly than WT cells.
source: We find no evidence that S47 LCLs and MEFs proliferate more quickly than WT cells (Jennis et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Jennis et al., 2016.

claim: The increased nutrient consumption in S47 cells may be used for biomass instead of proliferation.
source: this raises the possibility that this increased nutrient consumption may be used for biomass instead of proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a possibility based on the data.

claim: S47 cells are less susceptible to inhibition of oxygen consumption rate by rapamycin compared to WT cells.
source: Seahorse analysis of WT and S47 LCLs revealed that S47 cells are less susceptible to inhibition of oxygen consumption rate and maximal respiration by the mTOR inhibitors rapamycin (Figure 3A and B)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: S47 cells are less susceptible to inhibition of maximal respiration by rapamycin compared to WT cells.
source: Seahorse analysis of WT and S47 LCLs revealed that S47 cells are less susceptible to inhibition of oxygen consumption rate and maximal respiration by the mTOR inhibitors rapamycin (Figure 3A and B)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: S47 cells are less susceptible to inhibition of oxygen consumption rate by Torin1 compared to WT cells.
source: Seahorse analysis of WT and S47 LCLs revealed that S47 cells are less susceptible to inhibition of oxygen consumption rate and maximal respiration by the mTOR inhibitors rapamycin (Figure 3A and B) and Torin1 (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 3C and D.

claim: S47 cells are less susceptible to inhibition of maximal respiration by Torin1 compared to WT cells.
source: Seahorse analysis of WT and S47 LCLs revealed that S47 cells are less susceptible to inhibition of oxygen consumption rate and maximal respiration by the mTOR inhibitors rapamycin (Figure 3A and B) and Torin1 (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The differential susceptibility to mTOR inhibitors is not due to altered efficacy of the inhibitors in WT versus S47 cells.
source: This finding was not due to altered efficacy of each inhibitor, as evidenced by similar decreases in p-mTOR and p-S6 in WT and S47 cells following treatment with rapamycin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and Torin1 (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3E.

claim: Very high concentrations of Torin1 can inhibit oxygen consumption equally well in both WT and S47 cells.
source: and by the finding that very high concentrations of Torin1 were able to inhibit oxygen consumption equally well in both WT and S47 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is an S47 dependent, but mTOR-independent, effect on OCR.
source: These data support the possibility of an S47 dependent, but mTOR-independent, effect on OCR as well.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a possibility based on the data.

claim: There are no significant differences at the protein level of any p53-regulated mTOR regulators in steady state MEFs.
source: Unfortunately, although we identified decreased mRNA levels of some mTOR regulators in S47 cells, we found no evidence for significant differences at the protein level of any p53-regulated mTOR regulators in steady state MEFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or following treatment with Nutlin to induce p53 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: There are increased mTOR-Rheb complexes in S47 cells compared to WT.
source: PLA experiments revealed that there were consistently increased mTOR-Rheb complexes in S47 cells, compared to WT; this was true in multiple replicates, in multiple MEF clones, and using single antibody controls that showed no signal (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PLA data in Figure 4A.

claim: There is an approximately two-fold increase in mTOR-Rheb complexes in S47 cells compared to WT.
source: Quantification of multiple experiments revealed an approximately two-fold increase in mTOR-Rheb complexes in S47 cells compared to WT (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification data in Figure 4B.

claim: GAPDH binds to Rheb and sequesters it from mTOR in cultured cells in a manner regulated by glucose levels.
source: One regulator of the mTOR-Rheb interaction is the cytosolic enzyme GAPDH. This enzyme binds to Rheb and sequesters it from mTOR in cultured cells, in a manner that is regulated by glucose levels (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Lee et al., 2009.

claim: The interaction between Rheb and GAPDH is detectable in the skeletal muscle of mice and is regulated by glucose.
source: First, we confirmed that the interaction between Rheb and GAPDH is detectable in the skeletal muscle of mice using IP-western, and moreover that this interaction is regulated by glucose (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IP-western data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is increased mTOR in Rheb IPs from S47 skeletal muscle compared to WT.
source: Next, we performed immunoprecipitation (IP)-western of Rheb in skeletal muscle extracts from WT and S47 mice; we found that there was increased mTOR, and significantly decreased GAPDH, in Rheb IPs from S47 skeletal muscle compared to WT (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IP-western data in Figure 4C.

claim: There is significantly decreased GAPDH in Rheb IPs from S47 skeletal muscle compared to WT.
source: Next, we performed immunoprecipitation (IP)-western of Rheb in skeletal muscle extracts from WT and S47 mice; we found that there was increased mTOR, and significantly decreased GAPDH, in Rheb IPs from S47 skeletal muscle compared to WT (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IP-western data in Figure 4C.

claim: There is an approximately twofold decrease in the amount of GAPDH co-precipitating with Rheb in S47 skeletal muscle compared to WT.
source: The combined data from three independent IPs of Rheb in WT and S47 skeletal muscle revealed an approximately twofold decrease in the amount of GAPDH co-precipitating with Rheb in S47 skeletal muscle compared to WT (p<0.05, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification data in Figure 4D.

claim: There are no differences in the levels of mTOR, Rheb and GAPDH in WT and S47 skeletal muscle extracts.
source: In contrast, there were no differences in the levels of mTOR, Rheb and GAPDH in these extracts (Figure 4C – WCL, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The GAPDH-Rheb association is markedly decreased in S47 MEFs relative to WT MEFs.
source: Consistent with our IP-western findings, PLA analyses corroborated that the GAPDH-Rheb association is markedly decreased in S47 MEFs relative to WT MEFs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PLA data in Figure 4A.

claim: There are no significant differences in the cellular localization of Rheb at the lysosome in WT and S47 MEFs.
source: Confocal microscopy analyses revealed no significant differences in the cellular localization of Rheb at the lysosome, as assessed by LAMP1 localization, nor were there any differences in TSC2 localization at the lysosome in WT and S47 MEFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There are no differences in TSC2 localization at the lysosome in WT and S47 MEFs.
source: Confocal microscopy analyses revealed no significant differences in the cellular localization of Rheb at the lysosome, as assessed by LAMP1 localization, nor were there any differences in TSC2 localization at the lysosome in WT and S47 MEFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The increased mTOR activity in S47 cells may be due to increased Rheb-mTOR association caused by decreased association of Rheb with GAPDH.
source: The combined data support the premise that the increased mTOR activity in S47 cells may be due to increased Rheb-mTOR association, caused by a decreased association of Rheb with GAPDH.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion based on the data.

claim: GAPDH is a multi-functional enzyme that is sensitive to redox status.
source: GAPDH is a multi-functional enzyme that is known to be sensitive to redox status (Brandes et al., 2009; Chernorizov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to Brandes et al., 2009 and Chernorizov et al., 2010.

claim: Lung tissue and skeletal muscle from S47 mice possess increased GSH compared to WT tissues.
source: We first verified that lung tissue and skeletal muscle from S47 mice possess increased GSH compared to WT tissues, as assessed by an increased ratio of reduced versus oxidized glutathione (GSH:GSSG) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by GSH/GSSG ratio data in Figure 5A.

claim: DEM can successfully decrease the level of GSH and the GSH/GSSG ratio in S47 cells.
source: We then validated that the GSH alkylating agent diethylmaleate (DEM) could successfully decrease the level of GSH, and the GSH/GSSG ratio, in these cells (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by GSH/GSSG ratio data in Figure 5A.

claim: DEM treatment of immortalized S47 MEFs causes a dramatic decrease in markers of mTOR activity (p-mTOR and p-S6K1).
source: Notably, DEM treatment of immortalized S47 MEFs (iMEFs) caused a dramatic decrease in markers of mTOR activity (p-mTOR and p-S6K1), showing that modulation of GSH, even for as little as five hours, can impact mTOR activity (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: Modulation of GSH, even for as little as five hours, can impact mTOR activity.
source: Notably, DEM treatment of immortalized S47 MEFs (iMEFs) caused a dramatic decrease in markers of mTOR activity (p-mTOR and p-S6K1), showing that modulation of GSH, even for as little as five hours, can impact mTOR activity (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: The impact of DEM on mTOR activity is enhanced by the addition of glutamate.
source: Moreover, we found that the impact of DEM on mTOR activity was enhanced by the addition of glutamate, which decreases cystine import through system Xc(-), leading to decreased level of GSH (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: There are consistent differences in GAPDH cross-linking patterns in S47 samples compared to WT.
source: Notably, we found consistent differences in GAPDH cross-linking patterns in S47 samples compared to WT, as evidenced by altered mobility of GAPDH on SDS-PAGE of BMH-treated samples (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by BMH crosslinking data in Figure 5C.

claim: The altered mobility of GAPDH in S47 cells can be reversed following glutathione depletion by DEM treatment.
source: Moreover, the altered mobility of GAPDH in S47 cells could be reversed following glutathione depletion by DEM treatment (Figure 5C) or by the compound BSO (buthionine sulfoximine; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) which inhibits GSH biosynthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by BMH crosslinking data in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The altered mobility of GAPDH in S47 cells can be reversed by BSO which inhibits GSH biosynthesis.
source: Moreover, the altered mobility of GAPDH in S47 cells could be reversed following glutathione depletion by DEM treatment (Figure 5C) or by the compound BSO (buthionine sulfoximine; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) which inhibits GSH biosynthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by BMH crosslinking data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with erastin leads to altered mobility of GAPDH in S47 and WT cells.
source: Treatment with the compound erastin, which inhibits the system Xc(-) cystine transporter and decreases GSH, also led to altered mobility of GAPDH in S47 and WT cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by BMH crosslinking data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Supplementation of culture media with exogenous GSH decreases the Rheb-GAPDH interaction in WT cells.
source: By IP-western we found that supplementation of culture media with exogenous GSH decreased the Rheb-GAPDH interaction in WT cells
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IP-western data in Figure 5D.

claim: Depleting free GSH using BSO or DEM increases the Rheb-GAPDH interaction in S47 cells.
source: conversely, depleting free GSH using either BSO or DEM increased the Rheb-GAPDH interaction in S47 cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by IP-western data in Figure 5D.

claim: Depleting GSH using DEM or BSO completely restores GAPDH-Rheb complex formation in S47 cells to levels equivalent to WT cells.
source: These findings were corroborated using PLA, which revealed that depleting GSH using either DEM or BSO completely restores GAPDH-Rheb complex formation and mTOR-Rheb complex formation in S47 cells, to levels equivalent to WT cells (Figure 5E and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PLA data in Figure 5E, F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Depleting GSH using DEM or BSO completely restores mTOR-Rheb complex formation in S47 cells to levels equivalent to WT cells.
